title: A Secret Code in a 130-Year-Old Dress? The Answer Will Surprise You!
summary: Have you ever found a secret note and wondered what it meant? Now imagine finding one in a dress from the 1880s, full of words like "Bismark omit leafage buck bank." That's what happened to Sara Rivers Cofield when she bought an antique silk dress in Maine in 2013. Inside a hidden pocket, she found two crumpled papers covered in a strange code. For ten years, the world's best codebreakers tried to solve it. They called it the Silk Dress Cryptogram. Some thought it was spy messages, gambling codes, or even dress measurements. But the real answer is way more surprising—and a little bit funny. Wayne Chan, a data analyst and hobby codebreaker, finally cracked it. After searching through 170 old telegraph codebooks, he found a clue: the U.S. Army Signal Corps used a special weather code in the late 1800s. Each line on the paper was a weather report from a different station! So "Bismark omit leafage buck bank" actually means: in Bismarck, Dakota Territory, it was 56°F, clear skies, wind from the north at 12 mph. The code was used to send weather info by telegraph using as few words as possible. Chan even figured out the reports were likely from May 27, 1888. But who owned the dress? That's still a mystery. The name "Bennett" was on a label, but no one knows if she worked with weather reports. The dress has 130 years of secrets—and we've only solved one!
why_it_matters: It shows that solving puzzles can uncover hidden stories from history, and that even a simple dress can hold a 130-year-old mystery.

background_read: Before the telephone, the telegraph was the main way to send fast messages across long distances, using Morse code over wires.
The U.S. Army Signal Corps (the army's communication experts) created special codes to quickly share weather data so that people could prepare for storms.
Codes like the Silk Dress Cryptogram used nonsense words to replace whole weather descriptions, saving time and money on telegraph messages.

WHY: The code was a way to send weather information quickly and cheaply by telegraph, using fewer words.

perspectives.description: They find it thrilling that a modern puzzle-solver finally cracked a code that stumped experts for a decade, using old books.
They see it as a fascinating window into how 19th-century weather reporting worked, showing the cleverness of people before computers.
Some might laugh that a 'secret code' turned out to be boring weather data, but it still makes for a great mystery story.
